value.overview: The Roseate Tern (Sterna dougallii) is a slender, long-tailed seabird of warm and temperate ocean regions. It is named for the faint pink or rose-colored wash sometimes visible on the breast of breeding adults. The species nests in colonies on small islands and coastal islets, often among rocks or low vegetation, and feeds mainly on small fish captured from the sea. Several geographically separated populations occur across the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans.
value.classification: The Roseate Tern belongs to the tern family Laridae, order Charadriiformes. It is closely related to other Sterna terns, especially the Common Tern.
value.identification: A medium-sized, elegant tern with a deeply forked tail, narrow pointed wings, and a slim black bill. Breeding adults have a black cap, white forehead, pale gray back and wings, white underparts, and a long white tail; the bill commonly shows red at the base and black toward the tip. A subtle rosy flush may appear on the breast. Nonbreeding birds lose some black on the head and may show a darker bill. Juveniles are browner and more scaly above.
value.rangeHabitat: The Roseate Tern is widely distributed in tropical and temperate marine regions, nesting on small coastal islands, sandy cays, rocky islets, and low offshore vegetation. Outside the breeding season it uses coastal waters, bays, estuaries, and island shorelines. In Costa Rica it is an accidental species rather than a regular resident or migrant. A documented national record involved one bird at Bahía Soley, Playa Papaturro, Guanacaste, on September 20, 2015; occasional additional sightings may occur along either coast.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory in many populations. Atlantic breeders generally move south after breeding to Caribbean waters and northern South America, while other populations migrate within their ocean region. In Costa Rica, the species is considered accidental and has no established regular migration pattern.
value.breeding: Roseate Terns breed colonially, usually on predator-free islands or isolated coastal sites, sometimes nesting close to Common Terns and other seabirds. The nest is a shallow scrape on bare ground, sand, gravel, or among sparse vegetation. The usual clutch contains one or two eggs, and both parents incubate and feed the young. Adults defend nesting areas with aerial displays and sharp calls. Breeding success is strongly influenced by predators, storms, flooding, and disturbance at colonies.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small marine fish, with squid and other small marine animals taken when available. Roseate Terns usually forage in shallow coastal waters and over productive offshore areas, capturing prey by plunge-diving or dipping from flight. They may follow feeding fish, seabirds, or marine predators and can sometimes take food from other terns through brief aerial chases. Parents often transport fish crosswise in the bill to waiting chicks.
value.behavior: This tern is highly aerial and spends much of its time flying over the sea, often with graceful, buoyant wingbeats and sudden dives. It is social outside the breeding season and may roost with other terns on beaches, sandbars, or offshore rocks. At colonies it is vocal and territorial, using repeated calls while circling intruders. Roseate Terns commonly return to traditional nesting islands and show strong associations with established colony sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, with substantial variation among regions. Some Atlantic populations have recovered from historical hunting but remain relatively small and concentrated in a limited number of colonies.
